Technology T1 · Power transformer · Generator & HV motor · Cable terminations

Partial Discharge Monitoring

Shows whether an insulation defect is stable or growing, while the asset stays energised.

Partial discharge is a small electrical discharge that bridges only part of the insulation. It is both a symptom of an insulation defect and a cause of further damage.

Request a technical meeting ICMobserver datasheet

01The phenomenon

A small spark in the wrong place, thousands of times.

Insulation is designed to hold the full voltage across its thickness. A defect changes the local picture. A gas-filled void in solid insulation, a sharp edge, a contaminated surface: at such a point the electric field can exceed what the local material withstands, even though the insulation as a whole is far from breakdown.

The result is a discharge that bridges only that small region. It lasts a very short time and carries very little energy. The asset keeps working. But the discharge repeats with the alternating voltage, cycle after cycle, and each event erodes the material around it a little. The defect that causes the discharge is also enlarged by it.

That is why partial discharge is useful to measure. It is one of the few signs of insulation deterioration that can be observed from outside while the asset is in service.

Partial discharge is both the symptom and the cause.

Partial
The discharge does not bridge the whole insulation. There is no short circuit.
Repetitive
It follows the AC voltage and recurs on each cycle while the conditions hold.
Progressive
In solid insulation the damage is cumulative and does not heal.

02What it detects

A single measurement tells you discharge is present. A trend tells you whether to act.

D1

Voids and cracks

Voids, delamination and cracks inside solid insulation.

D2

Surface tracking

Surface discharges and tracking on bushings and terminations.

D3

Stator discharges

Slot and end-winding discharges in stator windings.

D4

Rising trend

Changes in discharge magnitude and repetition rate over time.

03Reading it

Three things to look at: how large, how often, where on the cycle.

Magnitude
How large the discharge pulses are. A rising level suggests a growing defect, but magnitude alone can mislead: a small, persistent discharge in a critical place can matter more than a large one somewhere harmless.
Repetition rate
How many discharge events occur per second. A defect that discharges more often is usually more active, even if the pulse size has not changed.
Phase position
Where on the AC voltage cycle the pulses occur. Different kinds of defect leave different patterns when pulses are plotted against phase. This is how internal discharges, surface discharges and external interference are told apart.
Trend
How all three change over weeks and months, and how they move with load, temperature and humidity. This is the part only continuous monitoring provides.

Noise

A substation or power plant is an electrically noisy place. Much of the work in online partial discharge measurement is separating real discharges inside the asset from interference outside it. Filtering, gating and pattern analysis exist for this reason, and a sudden “discharge” that does not follow the voltage cycle is usually not a discharge.

Limit — what it cannot tell you

  • The remaining life of the asset in months or years.
  • The exact location of a defect from a single measuring point.
  • Anything about failure modes that produce no discharge, such as purely thermal ageing.
  • Whether a level is “acceptable” without the asset’s own history as a reference.

Terms used on this page

AApparent charge, Qp and NQS3 terms

Apparent charge is the measured size of a discharge pulse as seen at the terminals, the quantity defined in IEC 60270. Qp is the peak apparent charge level; the basis of a level alarm. NQS is a measure of discharge activity per second; the basis of a rate alarm.

BPhase-resolved pattern, gating, coupler3 terms

A phase-resolved pattern is discharge pulses plotted against the AC voltage cycle. Gating is suppressing the measurement during known interference. A coupler is the sensor that picks up the discharge signal from the asset.

04Where it applies

Three assets, three different readings.

AssetWhat is monitoredWhat is different
Power transformerWindings and bushingsLong replacement lead time: early warning has the highest value here.
Generator and HV motorStator winding insulationA base level of partial discharge is normal in operation. The change over time is the useful signal, not the single reading.
Cable terminationsThe termination insulation and its interfacesThe weak point of a cable circuit is often where it ends.

Not for gas-insulated switchgear

Gas-insulated switchgear is monitored in the UHF range from inside the enclosure, with different equipment. On this site that row reads “On request”. Contact us if GIS is your asset.

05Product

Product · Megger, Power Diagnostix line

ICMobserver

A permanently installed partial discharge monitoring system from Megger’s Power Diagnostix product line.

Why two alarms

A level alarm catches a defect whose discharges are getting larger. A rate alarm catches one whose discharges are getting more frequent. Defects do not always do both.

Type
Permanently installed system for continuous online partial discharge monitoring
In one unit
Spectrum analyser, time-domain oscilloscope, voltage measurement, partial discharge monitor
Alarms
Two types: Qp alarm on discharge level; NQS alarm on the number of discharge events per second
Signal processing
Digital signal processing with noise gating for sites with strong interference
Operation
Through a web browser
Existing sensors
Partial discharge sensors already installed on an asset, including those from other suppliers, can typically be integrated
Sensors
Bushing couplers, coupling capacitors or UHF sensors, depending on the asset; defined with the manufacturer for each installation
Assets
Power transformers; rotating machines (generators, motors); cable terminations

06After an alarm

An alarm starts a check, not a shutdown.

  1. Step 1

    Check that it is real.

    Compare with the phase pattern, the other channels and what was happening on site. Interference is ruled out first.

  2. Step 2

    Look at the trend.

    Is the change a step or a slope? Does it follow load, temperature or humidity?

  3. Step 3

    Cross-check.

    On a transformer, look at dissolved gas and moisture. On a machine, look at operating data and the last offline results.

  4. Step 4

    Decide the next measurement.

    A targeted offline test or inspection at the next opportunity, or sooner if the trend is steep.

  5. Step 5

    Plan.

    Set the intervention at a time you choose.

General sequence. The operating procedure belongs to the asset owner.

07Related technology

One insulation system, seen from two sides.

Partial discharge shows the electrical condition of the insulation; dissolved gas monitoring shows what is happening in the oil. On power transformers the two are read together.

A rise in both is a stronger finding than a rise in either. A rise in one without the other is also information: it narrows down what kind of process is at work.

08Standards

Relevant standards

IEC 60270
The reference standard for partial discharge measurement.
IEC TS 62478
Electromagnetic (including UHF) and acoustic measurement methods.
IEC TS 60034-27-2
Online partial discharge measurement on stator windings of rotating machines.

Standards are named for orientation. They describe measurement methods, not acceptance limits for a specific asset.

09FAQ

Questions we are asked

Q1Is any partial discharge a problem?

Not necessarily. In rotating machines a base level is normal in operation. In all assets, the level is judged against the asset’s own history. What matters most is a change.

Q2Why monitor continuously if we already test periodically?

A periodic test records one moment. Discharge activity varies with load, temperature and humidity, and a defect can start after the test. Continuous monitoring records the trend between tests.

Q3Can monitoring tell us when the insulation will fail?

No. It shows that a defect is active and whether it is growing. It does not give a failure date. It gives time to investigate and plan.

Q4We already have couplers fitted on our generator. Can they be used?

Per manufacturer data, sensors already installed on an asset, including those from other suppliers, can typically be integrated with ICMobserver. This is confirmed for each installation.

Q5Is ICMobserver used for gas-insulated switchgear?

No. GIS is a separate case and is listed on this site as “On request”.
